prompt:
Many people today feel that they have less free time than previous generations did, even though technology has made many everyday tasks quicker and easier.

Why do people feel this way? What can be done to help people achieve a better balance between work and leisure?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
checklist: Explain WHY people feel they have less free time (the question is about the feeling, not only about working hours)
Address the paradox: technology saves time, yet people feel busier
Suggest what can be done to improve the work–leisure balance (by individuals, employers and/or governments)
Answer both questions with roughly equal development
Make your position clear in the introduction and conclusion

for: Smartphones and email blur the line between work and home: people are always reachable
Time saved by technology is filled with more tasks and higher expectations
Long commutes and rising living costs push people to work more hours
Leisure itself has become busy: social media and constant entertainment leave little real rest
against: Laws giving employees the right to disconnect outside working hours
Flexible working, four-day weeks or remote work to cut commuting time
Individuals setting limits: turning off notifications, scheduling free time
Employers measuring results rather than hours spent online

models.text:
It is something of a paradox that, in an age of dishwashers, online banking and instant messaging, so many people complain that they never have a moment to themselves. In my view, this feeling stems less from the amount of work people do than from the way technology has blurred the boundaries around it, and restoring those boundaries requires action from both employers and individuals.

The main reason people feel time-poor is that work no longer stays in the workplace. Smartphones mean that employees can be contacted at any hour, and many feel obliged to answer emails in the evening or at weekends, so that even their free time is interrupted by professional concerns. Secondly, the time that technology saves tends to be absorbed rather than enjoyed. When a report that once took a day can be produced in an hour, expectations simply rise, and people end up doing more tasks rather than finishing earlier. Finally, leisure itself has changed. Hours that previous generations might have spent reading or talking are now often filled with scrolling through social media, which leaves people feeling neither rested nor entertained.

Several measures could help to redress this balance. At the level of policy, governments could follow the example of countries such as France, where large companies must negotiate rules limiting work emails outside office hours. Employers, for their part, could judge staff on the results they achieve rather than on how quickly they reply to messages, and could offer flexible schedules or remote working, which eliminate long commutes. Ultimately, however, individuals also need to take responsibility, for instance by switching off notifications after a certain time and deliberately setting aside periods for activities that are genuinely restorative, such as exercise or time with family.

In conclusion, people feel they have less free time mainly because technology has allowed work and distraction to invade their private lives. A combination of clearer legal limits, more sensible workplace cultures and personal discipline would allow them to reclaim it.
models.commentary: Task Response (8): responde a las dos preguntas con el mismo peso y aborda directamente la paradoja del enunciado (la tecnología ahorra tiempo pero la gente se siente más ocupada), que es lo que distingue una respuesta de 8 de una genérica. Las soluciones se corresponden con las causas. Ejemplo concreto (la normativa francesa). Coherence & Cohesion (8): párrafo de causas con progresión clara (The main reason, Secondly, Finally) y párrafo de soluciones por niveles (gobierno, empresas, individuos). Lexical Resource (8): time-poor, blurred the boundaries, absorbed rather than enjoyed, redress this balance, genuinely restorative, reclaim. Grammatical Range & Accuracy (8): relativas, condicionales implícitas, so that, rather than + -ing, sin errores. Para un 9: algo menos de densidad en el párrafo de soluciones y un ejemplo personal o de empresa concreta.

models.text:
Although technology has made many tasks faster, a lot of people believe they have less free time than their parents or grandparents had. This essay will explain the reasons for this feeling and suggest some ways to improve the balance between work and leisure.

There are several reasons why people feel this way. First of all, modern technology allows people to work from anywhere at any time. For example, many office workers check their emails on their phones in the evening, so they never completely stop working. Another reason is that the cost of living has increased in many cities, which forces people to work longer hours or even have two jobs. In addition, many people spend hours commuting every day, which reduces the time they have for themselves. Finally, people today often try to do too many things in their free time, such as going to the gym, learning new skills and meeting friends, so they feel constantly busy.

However, there are some solutions to this problem. Firstly, companies should respect their employees' free time and avoid sending messages after working hours. Some countries have even introduced laws to protect this right. Secondly, employers could allow staff to work from home some days a week, which would save time on commuting. Lastly, individuals should learn to organise their time better and accept that they cannot do everything. For instance, they could turn off their phones in the evening and spend time on relaxing activities.

In conclusion, people feel they have less free time because of technology, long working hours and busy lifestyles. However, if companies and individuals make some changes, it is possible to achieve a healthier work–life balance.
models.commentary: Task Response (7): responde a las dos preguntas con ideas relevantes y ejemplos, pero no explora la paradoja del enunciado (por qué, si la tecnología ahorra tiempo, la gente se siente más ocupada); algunas causas (coste de vida, desplazamientos) no se relacionan con la tecnología. Coherence & Cohesion (7): estructura clara, aunque los conectores son mecánicos (First of all, Another reason, In addition, Finally, Firstly, Secondly, Lastly). Lexical Resource (7): vocabulario adecuado (cost of living, commuting, work–life balance), con poca precisión idiomática. Grammatical Range & Accuracy (7): buena variedad (relativas con which, condicionales) y errores mínimos. Para subir a 8: explicar la paradoja, reducir el número de ideas y desarrollar mejor cada una, y variar la cohesión.

models.text:
Nowadays technology helps us to do many things more fast, for example washing machines and computers. But many people think that they have less free time than before. In this essay I will explain why and what we can do.

The first reason is the mobile phones. People always have the phone with them and the boss can send messages in any moment. So people are working also at home and in the weekend. Another reason is that the life is more expensive now and people need to work more hours for pay the rent and the bills. Also people do many activities, like gym, English classes and social media, so they don't have time for relax. For example my sister works in an office and after work she goes to the gym and to French classes, so she never has a free evening and she is always tired.

There are some things that we can do. The government can make a law that the companies can't send emails after work. Also the companies can let the workers work from home, so they don't lose time in the transport. And the people need to organise better their time and do less things. For example they can turn off the phone in the night and do something relaxing, like read a book or walk in the park. I think this is the most easy solution because everybody can do it.

In conclusion, people feel that they don't have free time because of mobile phones, the expensive life and too many activities. The government, the companies and the people must do something to have a better balance between work and free time.
models.commentary: Task Response (6): responde a las dos preguntas, pero las ideas son generales y apenas se desarrollan (una o dos frases por idea, sin ejemplos concretos). Coherence & Cohesion (6): estructura correcta, pero la cohesión es repetitiva (Also, And, So) y algunos párrafos son listas de ideas. Lexical Resource (6): vocabulario sencillo y errores típicos del hispanohablante: in any moment (at any moment), for pay (to pay), for relax (to relax), the life is more expensive (life is more expensive / the cost of living has risen), lose time in the transport (waste time commuting). Grammatical Range & Accuracy (6): more fast (faster), organise better their time (organise their time better), do less things (fewer things), artículos innecesarios (the mobile phones, the people). Para subir a 7: desarrollar cada causa con una explicación y un ejemplo, y corregir artículos, comparativos y to + infinitivo.

prompt:
In many countries, a growing number of people are choosing to live alone rather than with family, friends or a partner.

Is this a positive or negative development?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
checklist: State clearly whether you think the trend is mainly positive, mainly negative, or mixed
Consider effects on individuals AND on society (housing, environment, health, community)
Note that the prompt says "choosing": focus on people who live alone by choice, not only on loneliness in old age
Support your position with reasons and examples
Acknowledge the other side before explaining why your view is stronger

for: Living alone reflects financial independence and personal freedom
People can focus on their careers, hobbies and personal growth
It allows people to leave unhappy relationships or crowded family homes
Many people who live alone have active social lives outside the home
against: Risk of loneliness and isolation, especially in old age, with effects on mental and physical health
More single-person households increase demand for housing and push up prices
Less efficient use of energy, land and resources per person
Weaker family ties and less informal care for children and the elderly

models.text:
In cities from Stockholm to Tokyo, single-person households are now among the most common type of home. While this trend reflects greater prosperity and personal freedom, I believe that its effects on society as a whole are, on balance, more negative than positive.

There is no doubt that choosing to live alone brings real benefits for many individuals. It is often a sign of financial independence, as only people with a stable income can afford their own home. It also gives people the freedom to organise their lives as they wish, to concentrate on demanding careers or to pursue interests without having to compromise with others. Furthermore, it enables people to leave relationships or family situations that make them unhappy, which was much more difficult for previous generations, especially women.

However, the wider consequences are more worrying. Firstly, the rise in single-person households has placed considerable pressure on housing. Because each person occupies a whole flat, cities need far more homes for the same population, and this contributes to rising rents and the spread of cities into the countryside. Secondly, living alone is less efficient in environmental terms: a person living by themselves consumes more energy and water per head than someone sharing a home, since heating, lighting and appliances are not shared. Finally, although many people who live alone have rich social lives, the arrangement can easily become isolating, particularly in later life or during periods of illness. Studies in several countries have linked loneliness to depression and heart disease, which ultimately places a burden on public health services.

In conclusion, although living alone can offer independence and personal fulfilment, its impact on housing, the environment and public health means that I consider it a largely negative development. Encouraging alternatives, such as co-living schemes that combine private rooms with shared spaces, could preserve the benefits while reducing the costs.
models.commentary: Task Response (8): posición clara (más negativo que positivo) mantenida en todo el ensayo, y distingue con inteligencia entre los beneficios para el individuo y los costes para la sociedad, lo que evita una respuesta superficial. Ideas desarrolladas con mecanismos causales (más hogares → más presión sobre la vivienda). Coherence & Cohesion (8): párrafo de concesión seguido de párrafo principal, con progresión lógica y referencias claras. Lexical Resource (8): single-person households, financial independence, compromise with others, per head, isolating, co-living schemes, places a burden on. Grammatical Range & Accuracy (8): estructuras complejas (Because each person occupies…, although many people who…) sin errores. La propuesta final de co-living es un cierre maduro que no contradice la postura.

models.text:
Nowadays, more and more people in many countries decide to live on their own instead of sharing a home with family members, friends or a partner. In my opinion, this trend has both positive and negative sides, but I believe the negative effects are more important.

On the one hand, living alone has some clear advantages. People who live alone have more freedom, because they can decide everything about their home and their daily routine without asking anyone else. For example, they can choose when to eat, sleep or invite friends. In addition, living alone can help people become more independent and responsible, since they have to pay all the bills and do all the housework by themselves.

On the other hand, there are several disadvantages. The most serious one is loneliness. People who live alone may spend many hours without talking to anyone, and this can lead to mental health problems such as depression. This is especially true for elderly people, who may have no one to help them if they become ill. Moreover, this trend has a negative effect on cities, because more people living alone means that more flats are needed. As a result, the price of housing goes up, and it becomes more difficult for young families to find an affordable home.

In conclusion, although living alone gives people freedom and independence, I believe it is mainly a negative development because it can cause loneliness and makes housing more expensive. Governments and communities should therefore find ways to help people who live alone stay connected with others.
models.commentary: Task Response (7): opinión clara y coherente, con argumentos relevantes a ambos lados. Sin embargo, se centra sobre todo en la soledad de los mayores, aunque el enunciado habla de personas que eligen vivir solas, y la idea del impacto ambiental no aparece. Coherence & Cohesion (7): estructura clásica bien ejecutada; conectores correctos pero predecibles (On the one hand, In addition, On the other hand, Moreover, As a result). Lexical Resource (7): adecuado (on their own, affordable, mental health problems), con algunas expresiones repetidas (live/living alone aparece siete veces). Grammatical Range & Accuracy (7): buena variedad, errores casi inexistentes. Para subir a 8: ajustar el argumento a quienes viven solos por elección, añadir un efecto social menos obvio y variar la referencia (this arrangement, single-person households).

models.text:
Nowadays many people choose to live alone. In my opinion this situation has good things and bad things.

First, the good things. When you live alone you have more freedom. You can do what you want in your house and nobody tell you what to do. For example you can listen music very loud or eat at any time. Also you learn to be independent because you have to cook, clean and pay the bills alone. This is very good for the young people. When I lived alone for one year in another city, I learned to cook and to organise my money, and now I am more responsible than before.

Second, the bad things. The people who live alone can feel very lonely, especially the old people. If they are sick, nobody can help them. In my country there are many old people that live alone and sometimes they have problems. Also living alone is more expensive, because you pay all the rent and the electricity yourself, and not everybody can do this. Another bad thing is that the houses are more expensive in the cities because everybody wants a flat.

In conclusion, living alone has advantages and disadvantages. I think it is positive for the young people and negative for the old people, so it depends of the age of the person. The government needs to help the old people that live alone, for example with visits or with activities in the neighbourhood.
models.commentary: Task Response (6): con unas 245 palabras no llega al mínimo de 250, lo que por sí solo ya penaliza este criterio. Además, presenta aspectos positivos y negativos con algún ejemplo, pero la postura sólo aparece al final y es ambigua (depende de la edad), y el ensayo se lee más como un ensayo de ventajas e inconvenientes que como una valoración. El argumento del precio de la vivienda se menciona pero no se explica. Coherence & Cohesion (6): organización clara (First, Second) pero párrafos que enumeran sin desarrollar. Lexical Resource (6): básico (good things, bad things, very) y errores: listen music (listen to music), depends of (depends on). Grammatical Range & Accuracy (6): concordancia (nobody tell → tells), artículos innecesarios (the young people, the old people), that para personas en relativa aceptable pero repetitivo, oraciones mayoritariamente simples. Para subir a 7: posición clara desde la introducción, desarrollar cada argumento y usar estructuras complejas.

prompt:
In a rapidly changing world, the ability to adapt is more valuable than specialist knowledge.

To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
checklist: Trap: this is a COMPARISON — say how far adaptability is MORE valuable than specialist knowledge; do not just praise adaptability
Define or illustrate what "adaptability" and "specialist knowledge" mean in practice
Consider whether the two are really opposites (adaptability may depend on deep knowledge)
Give a clear extent (completely, largely, partly) and keep it consistent
Use concrete examples (careers, industries, technology)

for: Specialist knowledge goes out of date quickly in fields like technology
Many jobs that exist today did not exist twenty years ago
Adaptable people can retrain and move between sectors when industries decline
Employers increasingly value problem-solving and learning ability over fixed skills
against: Some fields (medicine, engineering, law) still depend on deep, specialised expertise
Adaptation without knowledge is shallow: experts adapt better within their field
Societies need specialists to create the innovations that cause change
Deep knowledge itself teaches how to learn, which supports adaptability

models.text:
Few would deny that the pace of technological and economic change has accelerated in recent decades. It is therefore often argued that being able to adapt now matters more than mastering a particular field. I agree with this view to a large extent, although I would argue that the most adaptable people are often those who have first acquired deep knowledge of something.

The case for adaptability rests largely on how quickly specialised knowledge can become obsolete. A graphic designer trained in print layout twenty years ago, for example, would have needed to learn web design, then mobile interfaces and now, increasingly, how to work alongside image-generating software. Those who refused to adapt found their expertise in declining demand, however impressive it once was. The same pattern can be seen on a larger scale when entire industries, such as coal mining or film photography, shrink: workers who can retrain and transfer their skills to new sectors fare far better than those whose value depended on one narrow specialism. It is no coincidence that employers now routinely list the ability to learn quickly among the qualities they seek.

Nevertheless, it would be a mistake to see the two qualities as opposites. In many professions, such as surgery, structural engineering or air traffic control, there is no substitute for detailed expertise, and a merely flexible generalist would be dangerous. Moreover, deep knowledge often makes adaptation possible. A doctor with a thorough understanding of human biology can absorb new treatments far more readily than a layperson, precisely because new information can be connected to an existing framework. In this sense, specialist knowledge is not the alternative to adaptability but frequently its foundation.

In conclusion, I largely agree that adaptability has become the more valuable quality, since knowledge in many fields now has a limited lifespan. However, the ideal is not to choose between the two but to develop expertise in a way that equips people to keep learning throughout their lives.
models.commentary: Task Response (8): evita la trampa del enunciado: no se limita a elogiar la adaptabilidad, sino que compara las dos cualidades y matiza que no son opuestas, con una postura clara (to a large extent) mantenida hasta el final. Ejemplos concretos y bien explicados (diseñador gráfico, minería, cirugía). Coherence & Cohesion (8): cada párrafo tiene una función clara; Nevertheless y In this sense guían el razonamiento. Lexical Resource (8): obsolete, declining demand, fare far better, no substitute for, layperson, existing framework, limited lifespan. Grammatical Range & Accuracy (8): condicional perfecto (would have needed), relativas con whose, cleft (It is no coincidence that…), sin errores.

models.text:
Today, the world is changing faster than ever because of new technology and globalisation. Some people believe that being able to adapt is now more important than having specialist knowledge. I mostly agree with this opinion, but I think specialist knowledge is still essential in some areas.

There are several reasons why adaptability is so valuable nowadays. Firstly, knowledge in many fields becomes out of date very quickly. For example, a computer programmer who only knows one programming language may find it difficult to get a job when companies start using new technologies. Therefore, people who can learn new skills quickly have a big advantage. Secondly, many people now change jobs several times during their career, and some jobs disappear completely because of automation. In this situation, workers who can adapt to new roles are more likely to be successful than those who only have knowledge of one area.

On the other hand, specialist knowledge remains very important in certain professions. Doctors, pilots and engineers, for instance, need a high level of expertise to do their jobs safely, and adaptability alone would not be enough. Furthermore, new inventions and discoveries usually come from experts who have studied one subject in great depth, so society still needs specialists.

In conclusion, I believe that the ability to adapt is generally more valuable than specialist knowledge in the modern world, because jobs and technologies change so quickly. However, in some professions expertise is still vital, so the best situation is to have both.
models.commentary: Task Response (7): responde a la comparación con una postura clara (mostly agree) y ejemplos relevantes. Sin embargo, presenta las dos cualidades como si fueran independientes y no explora la relación entre ellas; la conclusión (lo mejor es tener ambas) es razonable pero algo previsible. Coherence & Cohesion (7): estructura sólida; conectores correctos pero mecánicos (Firstly, Secondly, Therefore, Furthermore). Lexical Resource (7): out of date, automation, expertise, in great depth; adecuado aunque poco sofisticado. Grammatical Range & Accuracy (7): buena variedad (relativas, more likely to), sin errores relevantes. Para subir a 8: analizar cómo el conocimiento especializado facilita la adaptación y desarrollar los ejemplos con más detalle.

models.text:
In the modern world everything is changing very fast, especially the technology. For this reason, some people think that adapt to the changes is more important than to have specialist knowledge. I agree with this idea.

First, the technology changes every year. For example, ten years ago nobody used the artificial intelligence, but now it is in all the jobs. If a person can not adapt, he will lose his job. My uncle worked in a bank for twenty years, but now the bank closed many offices and he had to find another job. He learned to use the computer and now he works in an online company. This shows that adaptability is very important.

Second, the people who are adaptable are more happy, because they are not afraid of the changes. They can travel, live in other countries and learn new things. The people who only know one thing have more problems when there is a crisis.

However, the specialist knowledge is also important for some jobs, like doctors. A doctor needs to know a lot about medicine. An engineer also needs to know a lot about buildings or machines. If they don't have this knowledge, it is dangerous for the people, so in these jobs the knowledge is more important than adapt.

In conclusion, I think that the ability to adapt is more important than specialist knowledge because the world changes very fast and we need to adapt. But for some jobs the specialist knowledge is still necessary.
models.commentary: Task Response (6): opinión clara y un ejemplo personal relevante, pero el enunciado pide comparar y el ensayo apenas trata el conocimiento especializado (dos frases en un párrafo muy corto). El segundo argumento (la gente adaptable es más feliz) se aleja de la pregunta. Coherence & Cohesion (6): estructura reconocible, pero párrafos desequilibrados y conclusión repetitiva. Lexical Resource (6): limitado y con errores: the technology, the artificial intelligence, the changes (artículos innecesarios), can not (cannot), more happy (happier). Grammatical Range & Accuracy (6): adapt to the changes is… (adapting to change is…), now the bank closed (has closed), oraciones mayoritariamente simples. Para subir a 7: dar el mismo peso a ambos lados de la comparación, mantener cada idea relevante y revisar artículos y gerundios.

prompt:
Some people think that the main purpose of art is to make the world a more beautiful place. Others believe that art should challenge people and even make them feel uncomfortable.

Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
checklist: Discuss the view that art exists mainly to create beauty
Discuss the view that art should challenge or disturb people
Give your own opinion (you may argue that art can do both, but say which matters more or when)
Note the word "main": the debate is about art's PRIMARY purpose
Use concrete examples of art (painting, music, film, architecture, literature)

for: Beauty gives pleasure, comfort and relief from daily stress
Public art and architecture improve the environment for everyone
Beautiful art attracts people of all backgrounds, not only experts
Much of the art that has lasted for centuries is admired for its beauty
against: Art can expose injustice and make people question their assumptions
War art, protest songs and political novels have changed public opinion
Discomfort can lead to empathy by showing other people's suffering
Art that only pleases can become decoration without meaning

models.text:
Art has been defined in countless ways, but much of the debate about its value comes down to a simple question: should it console us or confront us? While I recognise the importance of beauty, I believe that art fulfils its most valuable role when it challenges the way people see the world.

Those who argue that art should primarily create beauty have a strong case. Beautiful paintings, music and buildings give pleasure to millions of people, many of whom have no specialist knowledge, and offer a form of relief from the pressures of everyday life. A well-designed public square or a mural on a grey wall can lift the mood of an entire neighbourhood. Moreover, history suggests that beauty endures: people still travel across the world to see Renaissance frescoes or the Taj Mahal, not because these works make them uncomfortable but because they are moved by them.

On the other hand, many people believe that art has a duty to unsettle. Picasso's Guernica, with its distorted figures screaming in agony, is hardly beautiful in a conventional sense, yet it has done more to convey the horror of bombing civilians than countless newspaper reports. Similarly, novels such as those by Chinua Achebe or George Orwell have forced readers to confront colonialism and totalitarianism. By making audiences uncomfortable, such works encourage empathy and reflection, and sometimes even social change.

In my view, the two purposes are not mutually exclusive, and some of the greatest works achieve both. However, if art is designed only to please, it risks becoming mere decoration, pleasant but quickly forgotten. Its distinctive power lies in its ability to make people feel what they would otherwise ignore, and for that reason I believe challenging audiences is the more important of its aims.

In conclusion, beauty clearly enriches people's lives, but art matters most when it unsettles complacency and prompts people to think and feel differently.
models.commentary: Task Response (8): presenta ambas posturas con argumentos sólidos y ejemplos específicos (Guernica, Achebe, Orwell, el Taj Mahal) y una opinión clara que reconoce que ambos fines pueden coexistir pero indica cuál es más importante, respondiendo a la palabra main del enunciado. Coherence & Cohesion (8): introducción con pregunta retórica que enmarca el debate; transiciones naturales. Lexical Resource (8): console/confront, endures, unsettle, convey the horror, mutually exclusive, mere decoration, complacency. Grammatical Range & Accuracy (8): relativas (many of whom), not because… but because, participios y estructuras de énfasis, sin errores.

models.text:
Art plays an important role in every culture, but people disagree about its main purpose. Some believe that art should make the world more beautiful, while others think it should challenge people and make them uncomfortable. This essay will discuss both views before giving my own opinion.

On the one hand, many people believe that the main aim of art is to create beauty. Beautiful paintings, music and architecture make people happy and help them to relax after a stressful day. For example, many cities have beautiful parks, statues and old buildings that attract tourists and make residents proud of their city. In addition, beautiful art can be enjoyed by everyone, not only by experts, because people do not need special knowledge to appreciate it.

On the other hand, some people argue that art should make people think about serious problems. Art that shows war, poverty or injustice can make people feel uncomfortable, but it can also help them understand the problems of other people. For instance, many films and songs have raised awareness about issues such as racism and climate change, and some have even changed people's attitudes. Without this kind of art, people might ignore important social problems.

In my opinion, both purposes are valuable, but I believe that art which challenges people is more important. Although beautiful art makes life more pleasant, art that makes people question their ideas can have a bigger impact on society.

In conclusion, art can create beauty and also challenge people. While both views have merit, I think that the most important purpose of art is to make people think.
models.commentary: Task Response (7): discute ambas posturas y da una opinión clara, pero los ejemplos son generales (many films and songs) y la opinión personal se justifica en una sola frase. Coherence & Cohesion (7): estructura muy clara y equilibrada, con conectores correctos aunque predecibles. Lexical Resource (7): raised awareness, appreciate, injustice, have merit; vocabulario adecuado pero poco específico (beautiful se repite mucho). Grammatical Range & Accuracy (7): buena variedad (relativas, condicional con might, although) y errores mínimos. Para subir a 8: ejemplos concretos (una obra, un artista) y un párrafo de opinión más desarrollado.

models.text:
Nowadays art is very popular and there are many types of art like paintings, music and films. Some people think that art must be beautiful and others think that art must make people uncomfortable. In this essay I will discuss both opinions.

Firstly, art can make the world more beautiful. For example, when you go to a museum and you see a beautiful painting you feel happy and relaxed. Also the beautiful buildings in the cities are art and they are good for the people who live there. Many tourists visit my city because of the old churches and the monuments.

Secondly, some art is not beautiful but it makes people think. For example there are films about the war or about poor people, and when you watch them you feel sad and uncomfortable. But this is good because you learn about the problems in the world. Also some artists make strange art in the museums of modern art and the people don't understand it. In my opinion this art is not very useful, because if the people don't understand it, they can't learn nothing from it.

In my opinion, art must be beautiful, because the life is difficult and people need beautiful things to be happy. The art that makes people uncomfortable is also important but I prefer the beautiful art.

In conclusion, there are two opinions about art and both are important, but for me the most important is the beauty.
models.commentary: Task Response (6): con unas 243 palabras no llega al mínimo de 250, lo que por sí solo ya penaliza este criterio. Además, trata las dos posturas y da una opinión, pero las ideas son superficiales y la frase sobre el arte moderno que la gente no entiende no aporta al argumento. La opinión se basa en una preferencia personal (I prefer) más que en un razonamiento. Coherence & Cohesion (6): estructura correcta con Firstly/Secondly, aunque se usan para introducir puntos de vista y no argumentos. prompt:
Increasingly, decisions that were once made by people, such as who receives a bank loan or which job applicants are invited to an interview, are now made by computer programs.

Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
checklist: Discuss the advantages of computer programs making these decisions
Discuss the disadvantages
Answer the question directly: do the advantages OUTWEIGH the disadvantages? (a clear yes, no or "only if…")
Stay on topic: decisions ABOUT people (loans, hiring), not automation or robots in general
Use concrete examples or scenarios

for: Speed and efficiency: thousands of applications processed in minutes
Consistency: the same rules applied to everyone, without mood or fatigue
Potentially less personal prejudice than individual human decision-makers
Lower costs, which may be passed on to customers
against: Programs learn from past data and can reproduce past discrimination
Lack of transparency: applicants may not know why they were rejected
No room for exceptional circumstances or human judgement
Unclear responsibility when a decision is wrong

models.text:
Banks, employers and even public agencies now rely on software to sort applications and make judgements that were once the responsibility of trained staff. Although this offers clear gains in speed and consistency, I believe that, in their current form, these systems create risks that outweigh their benefits unless people remain closely involved.

The advantages are considerable. A program can process thousands of loan or job applications in the time it would take a human officer to read a handful, which reduces costs and allows applicants to receive an answer within minutes rather than weeks. Computers are also consistent: they apply identical criteria to every case and are not influenced by tiredness, mood or whether an applicant seems likeable. In theory, this should make decisions fairer, since human recruiters have repeatedly been shown to favour candidates who resemble themselves.

In practice, however, the promise of fairness is often not fulfilled. Most of these programs learn by analysing past decisions, so if a company has historically hired few women for technical roles, the software may conclude that being female is a negative factor and quietly reproduce that discrimination on a much larger scale. A second problem is transparency. Someone who is refused a mortgage by a bank manager can at least ask for an explanation, whereas an applicant rejected by a complex algorithm may never learn why, and therefore cannot correct a mistake or challenge an unfair outcome. Finally, programs struggle with exceptional circumstances, such as a career gap caused by illness, which a sensitive human reader would immediately understand.

For these reasons, I would argue that the disadvantages currently outweigh the advantages. Nevertheless, the solution is not to abandon such technology but to regulate it, for example by requiring companies to test their systems for bias and to guarantee that any applicant can have a decision reviewed by a person.

In conclusion, while automated decision-making is efficient and, in principle, consistent, its tendency to hide and multiply existing prejudices means that, without strong safeguards, its drawbacks are greater than its benefits.
models.commentary: Task Response (8): responde directamente a la pregunta outweigh (las desventajas pesan más, salvo con supervisión humana) y la condición se mantiene de forma coherente. Se ciñe al tema (decisiones sobre personas) en lugar de hablar de la automatización en general, que es el error más común aquí. Ejemplos concretos y razonados (sesgo en la contratación técnica, hipotecas, baja por enfermedad). Coherence & Cohesion (8): párrafo de ventajas, párrafo de desventajas con contraste In practice, y posición explícita. Lexical Resource (8): rely on, a handful, likeable, resemble, quietly reproduce, challenge an unfair outcome, safeguards. Grammatical Range & Accuracy (8): condicionales, pasivas (have repeatedly been shown), whereas, sin errores.

models.text:
Nowadays, many important decisions, such as whether someone gets a loan or a job interview, are made by computer programs instead of people. Although this development has some benefits, I believe that the disadvantages are more significant.

There are a number of advantages to using computer programs for these decisions. Firstly, they are much faster than humans. A bank can check thousands of loan applications in a few minutes, which saves time and money for both the bank and its customers. Secondly, computers are not affected by emotions. A human manager might reject a candidate because they are tired or in a bad mood, but a computer applies the same rules to everyone.

However, there are also serious disadvantages. The biggest problem is that computer programs can be unfair. They are designed using information about past decisions, so if people made unfair decisions in the past, the program may copy them. For example, if a company rarely employed older workers, the computer might automatically reject older applicants. Another disadvantage is that people often do not know why they have been rejected, so they cannot complain or improve their application. In addition, a computer cannot understand special situations, such as a person who has not worked for a year because they were caring for a sick relative.

In conclusion, although computer programs are fast and consistent, I believe the disadvantages outweigh the advantages, because they can be unfair and their decisions are difficult to understand. Therefore, I think humans should always check important decisions made by computers.
models.commentary: Task Response (7): respuesta clara a la pregunta y argumentos relevantes, bien ejemplificados. Algo menos de profundidad que un 8: no explica por qué las decisiones humanas tampoco son neutrales (lo que daría más peso a la ventaja de la consistencia), y la solución final aparece sólo en la conclusión. Grammatical Range & Accuracy (7): condicionales y pasivas correctos, sin errores relevantes. Para subir a 8: desarrollar más cada idea y usar léxico más preciso (bias, transparency, accountability).

prompt:
Many people today find it difficult to trust the information they read or hear, because so much misleading content is shared online.

What problems does this lack of trust cause for individuals and for society? What can be done to solve these problems?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
checklist: Trap: the problem to discuss is the LACK OF TRUST (people doubting everything), not only fake news itself
Explain problems for individuals (e.g. health decisions, anxiety, scams)
Explain problems for society (e.g. public health, elections, polarisation)
Propose realistic solutions linked to the problems you described
Develop both questions with roughly equal weight

for: Individuals ignore reliable advice, e.g. on vaccines or medicine
People may fall back on sources that confirm what they already believe
Public institutions find it harder to communicate in emergencies
Democracy suffers when citizens cannot agree on basic facts
against: Teach media literacy and source-checking in schools
Greater transparency from news organisations and governments (showing sources, correcting errors)
Platforms labelling or slowing the spread of unverified content
Supporting independent, well-funded public-interest journalism

models.text:
The spread of misleading content online has had a subtle but damaging side effect: many people now struggle to believe anything at all. This loss of trust, rather than misinformation itself, creates serious difficulties for both individuals and society, but it can be addressed through education, transparency and more responsible technology.

For individuals, the most immediate danger concerns decisions about health, money and safety. When people suspect that every source may be biased, they may dismiss sound medical advice as easily as false claims, or rely instead on whatever feels right, which leaves them vulnerable to unproven remedies and financial scams. Paradoxically, distrust often makes people more credulous, not less, because they abandon careful judgement and turn to sources that simply confirm their existing views. At a societal level, the consequences are equally serious. During a public health emergency, authorities depend on citizens following their guidance, and widespread suspicion can cost lives, as the hesitancy over vaccines in several countries during the recent pandemic illustrated. More broadly, democratic debate becomes almost impossible when citizens cannot agree on basic facts, which encourages polarisation and leaves people open to manipulation by extreme voices.

Rebuilding trust requires action on several fronts. Firstly, schools should teach media literacy as a core skill, showing students how to check where a claim comes from, compare sources and recognise manipulated images. Finland, which has done this for years, consistently ranks among the countries most resistant to misinformation. Secondly, trustworthy institutions must earn confidence by being open about their methods: news organisations that cite their sources and publicly correct their mistakes give audiences a reason to believe them. Finally, technology companies should be required to label unverified content and reduce the speed at which it spreads, rather than rewarding whatever attracts the most attention.

In conclusion, a general lack of trust undermines people's ability to make sound decisions and weakens society's capacity to act collectively. Education, transparency and regulation of online platforms together offer the best way to restore it.
models.commentary: Task Response (8): evita la trampa principal (habla de la falta de confianza, no sólo de las noticias falsas) y responde a todas las partes: problemas individuales, problemas sociales y soluciones, cada una con un ejemplo. La idea de que la desconfianza vuelve a la gente más crédula muestra un razonamiento maduro. Coherence & Cohesion (8): las soluciones responden a los problemas planteados; secuenciación clara y referencias precisas. Lexical Resource (8): side effect, dismiss sound advice, credulous, hesitancy, polarisation, media literacy, earn confidence, undermines. Grammatical Range & Accuracy (8): relativas, comparaciones (as easily as), pasivas y participios sin errores. Para un 9: el párrafo de problemas es muy denso y podría dividirse en dos.

models.text:
Nowadays, a large amount of false or misleading information is shared on the internet, and as a result many people find it hard to know what to believe. This lack of trust causes several problems, but there are also some possible solutions.

The first problem affects individuals. When people do not know which information is true, they may make poor decisions about their health or their money. For example, some people refuse to follow their doctor's advice because they have read something different online, while others lose money because they believe false investment advice. In addition, constantly doubting everything can make people anxious and confused. For society, the lack of trust is also dangerous. If citizens do not believe the government or scientists, it becomes very difficult to deal with problems such as pandemics or climate change. It can also divide society, because people with different opinions no longer share the same facts.

There are several ways to solve these problems. Firstly, schools should teach children how to evaluate information, for instance by checking the source and comparing different websites. Secondly, governments and news organisations should be more transparent and explain clearly where their information comes from, so that people can trust them again. Lastly, social media companies should remove false content more quickly and highlight reliable sources.

In conclusion, the lack of trust in information can lead to bad decisions by individuals and make it harder for society to solve problems. However, education, transparency and action by social media companies could help to rebuild trust.
models.commentary: Task Response (7): cubre todas las partes del enunciado con ideas relevantes y algunos ejemplos. Algunas ideas se quedan en lo general (no se menciona ningún caso o país concreto) y la solución de eliminar contenido no aborda del todo la desconfianza. Grammatical Range & Accuracy (7): condicionales y so that bien usados; sin errores importantes. Para subir a 8: un ejemplo concreto en cada parte, y relacionar mejor cada solución con un problema específico.

prompt:
In many countries, fewer people are taking part in traditional forms of community and civic life, such as voting in elections, joining local clubs or volunteering for neighbourhood organisations.

What are the reasons for this? What effects does it have on society?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
checklist: Explain several REASONS for lower participation (not just one)
Explain the EFFECTS on society (the question does not ask for solutions; a brief mention is optional, not required)
Cover the range of activities mentioned (voting, clubs, volunteering), not only elections
Note "traditional forms": you may mention that participation is shifting to new forms (online campaigns, petitions)
Develop both parts with roughly equal weight

for: Longer working hours, commuting and both parents working leave less free time
Moving frequently for work weakens ties to a local area
Distrust of politicians: people feel their vote makes no difference
Home entertainment and online communities replace local, face-to-face groups
against: Lower turnout means governments represent a narrower group (often older voters)
Fewer volunteers: local services such as sports clubs and food banks struggle
Weaker social ties increase loneliness and reduce mutual trust between neighbours
Civic energy moves online, which can be quick but shallow and polarising

models.text:
Across much of the developed world, polling stations, town halls and local sports clubs are noticeably emptier than they were a generation ago. This decline in traditional civic participation has several interconnected causes, and its consequences for social cohesion and democracy are, in my view, largely damaging.

One fundamental reason is the changing structure of working and family life. With longer hours, longer commutes and, in most households, both partners in paid employment, many adults simply lack the free evenings that membership of a choir or a residents' association demands. Greater mobility has a similar effect: people who move cities several times for work have little incentive to invest in a community they may soon leave. A further cause is political disillusionment. Many citizens, particularly younger ones, feel that elections change little and that politicians do not represent them, so voting comes to seem pointless. Finally, technology has provided alternatives to collective life, as people can find entertainment at home and join online communities built around shared interests rather than shared streets.

The effects of these changes are far-reaching. When turnout falls unevenly, governments are elected by a narrower and often older section of the population, so policies may increasingly neglect the concerns of young people and poorer groups, which in turn deepens their alienation. At a local level, the shortage of volunteers means that amateur sports teams, youth clubs and food banks struggle to survive, removing services that the state rarely provides. Perhaps most importantly, these institutions once brought together people of different ages and backgrounds who would otherwise never have met. Without them, neighbours become strangers, loneliness increases and trust between social groups weakens. Although some civic energy has moved online, into petitions and social media campaigns, these forms of participation are often brief and tend to connect like-minded people rather than bridging differences.

In conclusion, time pressure, mobility, political disillusionment and digital alternatives have all reduced participation in traditional civic life. The result is a society that is less representative, less supportive and more divided.
models.commentary: Task Response (8): explica varias causas bien desarrolladas y efectos que abarcan todas las actividades del enunciado (voto, clubes, voluntariado), sin desviarse hacia soluciones que no se piden. Grammatical Range & Accuracy (8): estructuras con with + sustantivo, relativas, condicional perfecto (would otherwise never have met), sin errores.

models.text:
In many countries, people are less involved in community activities than in the past. Fewer people vote in elections, join local clubs or volunteer in their neighbourhood. This essay will discuss the main reasons for this trend and its effects on society.

There are several reasons for this change. Firstly, many people are busier than before. They work long hours and spend a lot of time travelling to work, so they are often too tired to take part in community activities in the evening or at weekends. Secondly, many people have lost trust in politicians. They believe that their vote will not change anything, so they do not see the point of voting. In addition, people now have many forms of entertainment at home, such as streaming services and video games, and many prefer to communicate with people online instead of meeting them in local groups.

This trend has a number of negative effects on society. One effect is that governments may not represent everyone. If mainly older people vote, politicians may focus on their needs and ignore the problems of young people. Another effect is that many local organisations, such as sports clubs and charities, do not have enough volunteers, so they have to reduce their activities or close. Furthermore, when people do not take part in community life, they know fewer of their neighbours, which can lead to loneliness and a weaker sense of community.

In conclusion, people are taking part less in civic life because they are busy, they distrust politicians and they have other forms of entertainment. As a result, democracy becomes less representative and communities become weaker.

prompt:
It is often said that the most important qualities of a good leader cannot be taught.

What qualities do you think a good leader needs? Can these qualities be learned, or are people born with them?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
checklist: Identify specific qualities a good leader needs (two or three, well explained)
Answer the second question: can THESE qualities be learned, or are they innate?
Trap: the second question is about the qualities YOU named — connect the two parts
Give a clear position (learned, innate, or some of each — and which)
Use examples from work, politics, sport, education or personal experience

for: Qualities: integrity, the ability to listen, clear communication, calm decision-making under pressure, empathy
Skills such as public speaking, planning and delegation can clearly be taught
Leadership programmes, mentoring and experience improve people over time
Many leaders grew into the role rather than starting as natural leaders
against: Some traits linked to personality (confidence, charisma) seem partly innate
Integrity and empathy depend on character formed early in life
Courses cannot replace real experience of responsibility and failure
Some people never become good leaders despite extensive training

models.text:
The idea that leaders are born rather than made is a persistent one, partly because we tend to notice charismatic individuals who seem to command attention effortlessly. In my view, however, the qualities that matter most in a leader are largely developed through experience, even if some people begin with a natural advantage.

A good leader needs, above all, the ability to listen. Leaders who surround themselves with people who agree with them, or who dismiss bad news, tend to make costly mistakes, whereas those who genuinely seek out other perspectives can identify problems early. Secondly, a leader requires sound judgement under pressure: the capacity to make a decision with incomplete information and to take responsibility for the outcome. Finally, integrity is essential, because people will only follow someone they trust, and trust is quickly destroyed when a leader is seen to be dishonest or to apply one set of rules to others and another to themselves.

Whether these qualities can be learned is a more complex question, but I believe that they largely can. Listening, for instance, is less a personality trait than a habit, and it can be cultivated through feedback and practice; many companies now train managers to run meetings in which they speak last rather than first. Judgement improves with experience, which is why junior doctors and officers are gradually given greater responsibility instead of being placed in charge immediately. Integrity is perhaps the hardest quality to teach in a classroom, since it is shaped by upbringing and values, yet even here organisations can influence behaviour by rewarding honesty and setting clear examples from the top.

It is true that some traits, such as confidence or a commanding presence, appear to come more naturally to certain people. However, these are not the most important qualities, and they can even be dangerous when they are not accompanied by humility and good judgement.

In conclusion, a good leader needs to listen, to judge wisely and to act with integrity, and while personality may give some people a head start, these qualities are mainly acquired through practice, experience and example.
models.commentary: Task Response (8): responde a las dos preguntas y, sobre todo, las conecta: analiza si las cualidades que él mismo ha elegido se pueden aprender, una por una, en lugar de responder la segunda pregunta en abstracto. Posición clara y matizada (se aprenden en gran parte; algunas ventajas son innatas pero no las más importantes). Coherence & Cohesion (8): estructura paralela (cualidad → cómo se aprende) que da mucha cohesión; párrafo de concesión antes de la conclusión. Lexical Resource (8): command attention, costly mistakes, sound judgement, cultivated, upbringing, commanding presence, head start. Grammatical Range & Accuracy (8): relativas, comparaciones (less a… than a…), pasivas y concesivas (yet even here) sin errores.

models.text:
Leadership is important in many areas of life, such as business, politics and sport. Some people believe that the qualities of a good leader are natural and cannot be taught. In this essay, I will describe the qualities that I think a good leader needs and explain why I believe most of them can be learned.

In my opinion, a good leader needs three main qualities. The first is good communication. A leader must be able to explain goals clearly and motivate people to work towards them. The second quality is the ability to make decisions, especially in difficult situations, when there is no time to discuss every option. The third is honesty. If team members do not trust their leader, they will not follow him or her willingly.

I believe that most of these qualities can be developed. For example, communication skills can be improved through training and practice. Many people who are shy at first become confident speakers after taking courses or speaking regularly in meetings. Similarly, decision-making becomes easier with experience, as people learn from their mistakes. That is why most managers start with small responsibilities before leading large teams. However, honesty is more difficult to teach, because it depends on a person's character and values, which are formed during childhood.

On the other hand, some people are born with qualities such as confidence or charisma, which help them to become leaders more easily. Nevertheless, these natural qualities are not enough without experience and hard work.

In conclusion, a good leader needs communication skills, the ability to make decisions and honesty. Although some people have natural talents, I believe that most leadership qualities can be learned through education and experience.
models.commentary: Task Response (7): responde a ambas preguntas y relaciona las cualidades elegidas con la posibilidad de aprenderlas, con una posición clara. Las ideas son correctas pero algo previsibles y los ejemplos genéricos (many people who are shy…). Coherence & Cohesion (7): estructura muy clara (The first, The second, The third) que resulta algo mecánica. Lexical Resource (7): motivate, willingly, charisma, natural talents; adecuado aunque poco preciso. Grammatical Range & Accuracy (7): buena variedad (condicionales, relativas, as + cláusula), sin errores importantes. Para subir a 8: desarrollar más una idea original (por ejemplo, saber escuchar) y ejemplos concretos de cómo se entrena una cualidad.

In my opinion a good leader need to be intelligent, confident and honest. He need to be intelligent because he has to take important decisions. He need to be confident because the people follow a person who is sure. And he need to be honest because if not the people don't trust him. For example, a football captain needs to be confident and to speak to the team when they are losing.

I think that some qualities you are born with them and others you can learn. For example, the confidence is something that you have from the childhood. My brother was always very confident and now he is the boss in his company. But other things like speaking in public you can learn in a course. In my university we had a course of leadership and it was very useful. We learned how to speak in public, how to organise a team and how to solve problems. After the course many students were more confident. So I think that the training can help a lot, but it is not enough if the person is very shy.

In conclusion, I think that a good leader need some qualities and some of them are natural and some of them you can learn. Both are important.
models.commentary: Task Response (6): responde a las dos preguntas, pero no relaciona con claridad las cualidades que nombra (inteligencia, confianza, honestidad) con la segunda pregunta: habla de hablar en público, que no estaba en su lista. La posición es vaga (algunas sí, algunas no) y los ejemplos personales se quedan en anécdota. Coherence & Cohesion (6): estructura correcta, pero repetición constante de He need… y referencias confusas (it, them). Lexical Resource (6): limitado y con errores: take decisions (make decisions), a course of leadership (a leadership course), from the childhood (since childhood). Grammatical Range & Accuracy (6): concordancia repetida (a good leader need → needs), pronombre redundante (some qualities you are born with them), artículos innecesarios (the politics, the confidence). Para subir a 7: analizar cada cualidad elegida respecto a si se aprende y corregir la tercera persona del presente.

prompt:
Many people now record and share almost every part of their daily lives online, from what they eat to where they go on holiday.

Why do people do this? Is this a positive or negative development?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
checklist: Trap: there are TWO questions — explain WHY people share their lives online AND evaluate it
Give a clear judgement: positive, negative or mixed (and why)
Focus on ordinary people sharing everyday life, not only influencers or social media in general
Consider effects on the individual (well-being, privacy) and on relationships or society
Support with reasons and examples

for: Reasons: desire for approval (likes), staying in touch with distant friends and family, habit created by app design, creating a personal record or diary
Positive: keeps relationships alive across distances
Positive: creativity and self-expression; small businesses can grow
Positive: a shared record of everyday life and memories
against: Negative: constant comparison harms self-esteem, especially among teenagers
Negative: loss of privacy; data used by companies or criminals
Negative: experiences are lived for the camera rather than enjoyed
Negative: children's lives shared by parents without their consent

models.text:
Photographs of breakfast, updates from the gym and live videos from holidays have become an ordinary part of many people's online lives. This habit has several understandable causes, but I believe that, overall, its effects are more negative than positive.

The most obvious reason people share so much is the desire for recognition. Each like or comment provides a small sense of approval, and social media platforms are deliberately designed to encourage users to return for more of this reward. However, there are also more benign motives. For people living far from family and friends, posting everyday moments is a simple way of staying part of each other's lives; a grandmother in another country can watch her grandchildren grow up through regular photographs. Some people also treat their profiles as a kind of public diary, a record of experiences they want to remember.

These benefits are real, but they come at a considerable cost. Firstly, a constant stream of carefully selected images encourages comparison. Viewers see only the best moments of other people's lives and may conclude that their own are dull, which helps to explain why research has linked heavy social media use to anxiety and low self-esteem among teenagers. Secondly, recording everything changes the experience itself. At concerts or in famous places, many people now spend more time filming than looking, so the purpose of the activity becomes the post rather than the moment. Finally, there is the issue of privacy. Information about where people live, travel and spend their time can be collected by companies for advertising or exploited by criminals, and children whose parents post about them have no say in the matter.

In conclusion, people share their daily lives online largely to gain approval, but also to stay connected and to preserve memories. While these last two motives are valuable, the damage to self-esteem, to the quality of experiences and to privacy leads me to view the trend as a largely negative one.
models.commentary: Task Response (8): responde a las dos preguntas (por qué y valoración) con el mismo peso y una postura clara y mantenida. Distingue entre motivos egoístas y legítimos, lo que da credibilidad a la valoración final. Ejemplos concretos (la abuela, los conciertos, los hijos sin voz). Coherence & Cohesion (8): primer párrafo de causas, segundo de efectos con concesión inicial (These benefits are real, but…), conclusión que retoma ambas partes. Lexical Resource (8): desire for recognition, deliberately designed, benign motives, carefully selected, dull, exploited, have no say. Grammatical Range & Accuracy (8): relativas, explicación con which helps to explain why, comparativas, sin errores.

models.text:
Today, many people post details of their daily lives on social media, including their meals, their activities and their holidays. This essay will explain why people do this and argue that, although it has some benefits, it is mainly a negative development.

There are several reasons why people share so much online. One reason is that they want attention and approval from others. When people receive likes and positive comments, they feel popular and happy, so they continue posting. Another reason is that social media helps people to stay in contact with friends and relatives who live far away. For example, students who study abroad often post photos so that their families can see what they are doing. In addition, some people simply enjoy taking photos and creating content as a hobby.

Sharing everyday life online has some positive effects. It helps people maintain relationships and allows them to express their creativity. However, I believe the negative effects are more serious. Firstly, people who see the perfect lives of others online may feel that their own lives are boring, which can lead to unhappiness and low self-confidence, especially among young people. Secondly, sharing personal information can be dangerous. For instance, if someone posts that they are on holiday, criminals may know that their house is empty. Moreover, some people become so focused on taking photos that they do not really enjoy the moment.

In conclusion, people share their daily lives online because they want approval, wish to keep in touch with others and enjoy being creative. Although this can strengthen relationships, I think it is mostly negative because it can harm people's self-esteem and privacy.
models.commentary: Task Response (7): responde a las dos preguntas con una postura clara. Los aspectos positivos se tratan en sólo dos frases, por lo que la valoración parece algo desequilibrada, y algunas ideas se mencionan sin desarrollarse (no disfrutar el momento). Coherence & Cohesion (7): estructura lógica, conectores correctos aunque mecánicos (One reason, Another reason, In addition, Firstly, Secondly, Moreover). Lexical Resource (7): approval, stay in contact, self-confidence, keep in touch; adecuado. Grammatical Range & Accuracy (7): buena variedad (so that, so… that, condicionales) con errores mínimos. Para subir a 8: desarrollar más los aspectos positivos antes de rebatirlos y añadir algún dato o caso más concreto.

models.text:
Nowadays many people share all their life on the internet, for example photos of food, of their holidays or of their friends. In this essay I will explain why and if it is positive or negative.

People do this because they want to be popular. When you post a photo and you receive many likes you feel good. Also they want to show to the other people that they have a good life. Another reason is that it is very easy, because everybody has a smartphone with a good camera.

In my opinion this is negative. First, it is dangerous for the privacy. If you put all your life on the internet, everybody can see where you live and where you are, and this can be a problem. Second, people compare their life with the life of the others and they feel bad. For example my cousin is always looking the photos of influencers and she is sad because she doesn't have the same clothes. Also people don't enjoy the moment because they are always with the phone.

But there are some positive things, for example you can talk with your family if they live in other country. My aunt lives in Germany and we see the photos of her children every week, so we feel near. Also some people use the internet to show their art or their business.

In conclusion, people share their life because they want to be popular, and I think this is negative for the privacy and for the happiness of the people.
models.commentary: Task Response (6): responde a ambas preguntas con una opinión clara, pero los motivos son superficiales y el ejemplo de la prima habla de influencers, no de la gente que comparte su vida cotidiana. El párrafo positivo es breve y llega después de haber dado ya la opinión. Coherence & Cohesion (6): estructura básica; párrafo positivo suelto y mal integrado (But al inicio). Lexical Resource (6): limitado y con errores: dangerous for the privacy (a risk to privacy), show to the other people (show other people), looking the photos (looking at), in other country (in another country). Grammatical Range & Accuracy (6): artículos innecesarios (the privacy, the others, the happiness of the people) y oraciones mayoritariamente simples. Para subir a 7: explicar mejor los motivos, integrar los aspectos positivos y revisar preposiciones y artículos.
